overview: Pyu cities and communities developed in the dry Irrawaddy basin of present-day Myanmar. This shared card follows their urban history and later cultural legacy, not one uninterrupted kingdom. The atlas repeats the same broad outline for 800 to 900 and 1100 to 1279, enclosing Halin, Beikthano, Sri Ksetra and also Pagan. The later interval belongs to the Pagan period: surviving Pyu writing does not establish a separate Pyu state then. These imported dates and borders cannot serve as a founding date, conquest date or precise political frontier.

periods.title: Later Pyu urban history
periods.summary: This atlas slice follows centuries of city building; the earlier excavated households below are explicitly dated.

periods.title: Pyu language under Pagan rule
periods.summary: Early twelfth-century writing preserves Pyu in a Pagan royal dedication. The map label does not establish separate sovereignty.

items.text: Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra preserve brick walls, moats, religious monuments and waterworks. UNESCO places their broader urban tradition between about 200 BCE and 900 CE. Craftspeople worked iron, precious metals, terracotta and semiprecious stones, linking monumental building with many kinds of skilled work.

Four inscribed burial urns discovered near Sri Ksetra’s Payagyi stupa in 1911 preserve names and dates, probably of rulers. But which calendar starts the year count? Scholars disagree, and another urn complicates the supposed family sequence. Turning a carved number into a modern date can require a whole historical detective story.

At Sri Ksetra’s Bawbawgyi monument, tablets bearing the eleventh-century Pagan ruler Anawratha’s name provide evidence of later royal involvement. Hudson and Lustig interpret the deposit as a growing kingdom marking its territory ritually. The tablets themselves do not prove the much later chronicles’ story that he destroyed the city.

sections.title: Floors, food and the people who made them

items.text: In 2015, excavators at Sri Ksetra’s Yahanda mound discovered that an apparently natural hard layer was a stack of human-made work floors. People mixed sandy silt, clay, tiny potsherds, gravel and water, then let the sun harden it. The dated sequence runs from the mid-fifth through late-seventh century, probably into the eighth.

Those floors held food spills, cooking charcoal, iron nails and fragments of plain and cord-marked household pottery. A kitchen mess had become archaeological evidence! Across repeated rebuilding, the hard surfaces accumulated to about 60 to 70 centimeters in thickness. These earlier traces reveal household activity before the atlas’s 800 start.

A still older, pre-fifth-century dwelling at Yahanda had a wooden floor and postholes above a burial terrace. One posthole reached a cremation burial. Living and burial spaces could overlap here, although this single example cannot identify relatives or prove exactly why the builders chose that spot.

Brickmakers drew fingers through soft clay before drying and firing it, commonly leaving two or three parallel grooves. Such bricks occur at Pyu and Mon sites. The marks preserve a shared craft, rather than reliably identifying a maker’s language.

A study of rice chaff in 82 old brick samples found rounded, early-maturing grains prominent at Pyu sites and Pagan. The samples lacked independent dating. Even building materials can preserve food clues, though they cannot reconstruct everyone’s meals.

Outside Sri Ksetra’s western and southern walls, researchers traced a drainage channel running parallel to them for eight kilometers. Walls and moats helped manage water as well as shape the city. This is landscape drainage evidence; it does not establish household sewers, flushing toilets or a particular washing routine.

A silver coin catalogued by the British Museum as Pyu, around the sixth century, is only 20 millimeters across and weighs 2.28 grams. It carries a rising sun and an auspicious srivatsa design. This museum object predates the atlas interval; its record does not give a secure excavated findspot.

A 2025 study compared 245 full-unit Rising Sun/Srivatsa coins from regional museum collections. Matching tiny details can identify coins struck with the same die. One match links a coin found in eastern Bangladesh with another from Oc Eo in Vietnam, revealing far-reaching circulation. A shared coin design does not mean those places formed one Pyu empire.

sections.title: Pyu words in a later royal dedication

items.text: The early twelfth-century Myazedi pillars at Pagan preserve a royal dedication in Pyu, Old Burmese, Old Mon and Pali. Comparing their versions helps scholars decipher Pyu. These are evidence for skilled multilingual writing; they do not tell us that every family could read or that children all followed one school curriculum.

The Pyu face opens “siri”, glossed “Glory!”; line 4 contains “saḥ”, meaning “son”. These are scholarly Latin transliterations of the early twelfth-century inscription, not reproductions of its original letterforms. Miyake identifies siri as a Pali borrowing. Two little words connect religious praise and family relationships.

The dedication recalls Prince Rajakumar making a gold Buddha image for his sick father, King Kyansittha. It also records the endowment of three villages with enslaved workers. Family devotion, religious merit and coercive labor appear together in this Pagan-era document; the account does not establish a medical treatment or cure.

The associated Kubyaukgyi temple has a dark central shrine and a corridor lit through perforated stone windows. Builders shaped a visitor’s experience with light as well as brick. This is a Pagan-period setting for the Pyu-language dedication, rather than a building assigned to an independent twelfth-century Pyu kingdom.

ending.text: Pyu urban communities did not disappear together at a single atlas cutoff. Pagan authority became visible at older sites, while Pyu remained a written language in an early twelfth-century royal dedication. The map’s 900 and 1279 endpoints therefore should not be read as two documented falls of one Pyu kingdom.
